questions.q: Why is the most recent backup not automatically the safe one to restore from during incident recovery?
options: A backup taken after the attacker already had access can contain the attacker's changes, reintroducing the compromise when restored
Recent backups are always smaller in file size and therefore unreliable
Backup software only works correctly on backups older than 30 days
The most recent backup is always encrypted and cannot be restored at all
questions.explain: If a backup was captured after the attacker gained access, restoring it can reintroduce the compromise, disguised as a normal restore.

questions.q: In the Meridian scenario, why did the team restore the 1:00 AM Tuesday backup instead of the 1:00 AM Wednesday backup?
options: The earliest confirmed compromise was at 11:40 PM Tuesday, so the Wednesday backup was captured after the attacker already had access, while the Tuesday backup predated it
The Wednesday backup file was corrupted and could not be opened
Tuesday backups are always preferred over Wednesday backups as a company policy
The database server had no backup job scheduled for Wednesday at all
questions.explain: The backup has to predate the confirmed compromise timestamp from the investigation's own timeline, not just be the most recent one on the calendar.

questions.q: Why does Meridian's team still scan and integrity-check the backup even after confirming it predates the compromise timestamp?
options: A backup that predates the confirmed compromise could still miss an earlier, undetected stage of the same intrusion, or could have been tampered with after capture
Scanning backups is only required by compliance paperwork, not for security reasons
Integrity checks are unnecessary once a backup's date has been confirmed
Backups cannot be restored at all without first being rescanned
questions.explain: Predating the compromise narrows the field but doesn't guarantee the backup is clean or untampered — it still has to be verified.

questions.q: What makes a backup service account a high-value target, and why does that matter for trusting a backup?
options: It often has broad, domain-level access to read every server it backs up, so if an attacker compromises it, they could tamper with or corrupt backups independent of timing
Backup service accounts never have any special permissions at all
Backup service accounts are automatically disabled during any incident
Backup service accounts only affect email systems, not file or database backups
questions.explain: If the attacker's lateral movement reached the backup service account's credentials, a backup's old timestamp alone doesn't guarantee it's untampered.

questions.q: What is a 'known-good backup' as defined in this lesson?
options: A backup confirmed to predate the earliest confirmed compromise timestamp and verified clean through scanning and integrity checks
Any backup that is less than 24 hours old
A backup stored on a different physical server than the original
A backup that an end user has personally reviewed for suspicious files
questions.explain: Age alone isn't enough — a known-good backup has to both predate the confirmed compromise and pass verification.
